A model learns only from the table it is given. If that table holds a salinity of
−999, twelve spellings of four seabed types or the same site counted as five separate
observations, the model learns from those too, and nothing in its output says so.
Preparing the data takes most of the work in machine learning, and most of the
mistakes that invalidate a result are made there.

This section introduces the simulated coastal survey that the rest of the course works
on, then takes its raw file, as it came off the ship, to a table ready for a model: the
kinds of variable in its columns, the checks that find its problems and the fix for
each, the scaling and encoding that many methods need, and the split that keeps some
stations back to test a model. The pages build on each other, so read them in order.

The section ends on **information leakage**: information from the test set reaching the
model before it is tested, which makes the model look better than it is and gives no
warning. Every later section depends on avoiding it,
[Model validation and performance assessment](../07-validation/index.qmd) most of all.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [Preprocess your data with recipes](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/recipes/), tidymodels. A recipe built one step at a time.
- [recipes reference](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/), tidymodels. Every `step_*()` there is, which is the fastest way to find out whether the transformation you want already exists.
- [Preprocessing data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html) and [imputation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/impute.html), scikit-learn user guide.
- [Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html), scikit-learn. The leakage section is the best short statement of the problem this section ends on.
